## The short version

In October 1962, the United States and the Soviet Union came closer to nuclear war than at any other time in the Cold War. The U.S. State Department's historians describe it as [the moment when the two superpowers came closest to nuclear conflict](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1961-1968/cuban-missile-crisis).

The whole thing took 13 days. The most dangerous day was the last Saturday, October 27, 1962, which people now call "Black Saturday." On that one day, things went wrong in Washington, Moscow, Havana, the Arctic and the Atlantic Ocean at the same time.

This post is a plain-English timeline. It has three big tables:

- the 13 days, one row per day;
- Black Saturday, broken out by place and by time of day;
- the aftermath.

Near the end there is a table of places where the sources disagree, and a list of claims I could not confirm.

**How to read the sources.** Every row has a source link. I leaned on the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library's day-by-day pages, the U.S. State Department Office of the Historian, the National Security Archive at George Washington University, the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) day-by-day series, and a Defense Media Network article. Where I could not tie a statement to a source I read, I say so with a flag that starts with "Not confirmed."

**A note on time.** Most clock times below are Washington time. Moscow is several hours ahead, so a message sent "in the evening" in Washington could arrive in the middle of the night in Moscow.

## How it started (July to October 14)

| Date | What happened | Where | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| July 1962 | Khrushchev and Castro reach a secret agreement to put Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba. The stated aim was to deter another U.S. attempt to overthrow Castro | Moscow and Havana | [State Dept.](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1961-1968/cuban-missile-crisis) |
| Late summer 1962 | Construction of several missile sites begins in Cuba | Cuba | [State Dept.](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1961-1968/cuban-missile-crisis) |
| September 4, 1962 | Kennedy publicly warns against putting offensive weapons into Cuba | Washington | [State Dept.](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1961-1968/cuban-missile-crisis) |
| September 18 and 25, 1962 | Soviet military leaders report plans to send submarines to Cuba. The September 25 report plans one nuclear torpedo for each submarine | Moscow | [National Security Archive](https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/briefing-book/russia-programs/2022-10-03/soviet-submarines-nuclear-torpedoes-cuban-missile-crisis) |
| October 1, 1962 | Four Soviet Foxtrot-class submarines, each carrying one nuclear-armed torpedo, leave their base in Kola Bay | Soviet Arctic coast | [National Security Archive](https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/briefing-book/russia-programs/2022-10-03/soviet-submarines-nuclear-torpedoes-cuban-missile-crisis) |

The pilot is named as Major Richard Heyser in the title of a [CFR article](https://www.cfr.org/articles/major-richard-s-heysers-u-2-mission-discovers-soviet-missiles-in-cuba). I did not read the full article |

## The 13 days, one row per day

The JFK Library counts October 16 as Day 1 and October 28 as Day 13. Its pages are the backbone of this table.

| Day | Date | Washington | Moscow, Havana, UN and the sea | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Tue, Oct 16 | Kennedy and top officials are briefed on the U-2 photos. Two main options come up: an air strike and invasion, or a naval quarantine. Kennedy keeps his public schedule so the press does not notice | Nothing public yet | [JFK Library](https://microsites.jfklibrary.org/cmc/oct16/). State Dept. says the photos reached the White House the day before. A Foreign Relations of the U.S. summary says [McGeorge Bundy told Kennedy at 8:45 a.m. and a meeting was called for 11:45 a.m.](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1961-63v10-12mSupp/summary-xi) |
| 2 | Wed, Oct 17 | U.S. units start moving to bases in the Southeast. Another U-2 flight shows more sites. Kennedy attends a National Day of Prayer service, then goes to Connecticut to support Democratic candidates | None | [JFK Library](https://microsites.jfklibrary.org/cmc/oct17/) |
| 3 | Thu, Oct 18 | Kennedy meets Soviet Foreign Minister Andrei Gromyko. Gromyko says Soviet aid to Cuba is purely defensive. Kennedy does not reveal what he knows. He reads Gromyko his September 4 warning | Gromyko in the Oval Office | [JFK Library](https://microsites.jfklibrary.org/cmc/oct18/) |
| 4 | Fri, Oct 19 | Kennedy leaves on a scheduled campaign trip to Ohio and Illinois. His advisers keep debating in Washington | None | [JFK Library](https://microsites.jfklibrary.org/cmc/oct19) |
| 5 | Sat, Oct 20 | Kennedy returns early from Chicago. After about five hours of discussion he decides on the quarantine. He and his doctor use a fake cold as the reason for coming back | None | [JFK Library](https://microsites.jfklibrary.org/cmc/oct20/) |
| 6 | Sun, Oct 21 | After church, Kennedy hears from General Walter Sweeney of Tactical Air Command that an air strike could not guarantee 100% destruction of the missiles | None | [JFK Library](https://microsites.jfklibrary.org/cmc/oct21) |
| 7 | Mon, Oct 22 | Kennedy calls former Presidents Hoover, Truman and Eisenhower and British Prime Minister Macmillan. He formally creates the ExComm. He writes to Khrushchev. At 7:00 p.m. he goes on television, reveals the missiles and announces a naval quarantine. About an hour earlier, Secretary of State Dean Rusk tells Ambassador Dobrynin what the speech will say | Letters delivered in Washington and Moscow | [JFK Library](https://microsites.jfklibrary.org/cmc/oct22/). The State Dept. says Kennedy warned that any missile launched from Cuba would be treated as a Soviet attack needing a full retaliatory response, and that U.S. forces went to [DEFCON 3](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1961-1968/cuban-missile-crisis) |
| 8 | Tue, Oct 23 | Kennedy signs Proclamation 3504, authorizing the quarantine. The Organization of American States backs it. Kennedy asks Khrushchev to hold Soviet ships back. Robert Kennedy meets Dobrynin that evening | At the UN, Adlai Stevenson lays out the U.S. case. Quarantine ships take position. Soviet submarines move into the Caribbean area. Soviet freighters stop. The tanker Bucharest keeps going | [JFK Library](https://microsites.jfklibrary.org/cmc/oct23/) |
| 9 | Wed, Oct 24 | ExComm meets | Khrushchev replies angrily. He says Kennedy is making an ultimatum, not a quarantine. Some Soviet ships turn back, and others are stopped and allowed through | [JFK Library](https://microsites.jfklibrary.org/cmc/oct24/), [State Dept.](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1961-1968/cuban-missile-crisis) |
| 10 | Thu, Oct 25 | Kennedy drafts a letter to Khrushchev by hand. He knows some missiles are now operational. He rejects a UN cooling-off period because it would leave the missiles in place | At the UN, Stevenson confronts Soviet Ambassador Valerian Zorin with photos. Soviet freighters turn back. The Bucharest is allowed through. UN Secretary-General U Thant calls for a pause | [JFK Library](https://microsites.jfklibrary.org/cmc/oct25/) |
| 11 | Fri, Oct 26 | Morning ExComm: Kennedy predicts the missiles will only leave if the U.S. invades or trades. Soon after noon, KGB station chief Alexander Fomin (real name Aleksandr Feklisov) calls ABC reporter John Scali and offers a deal over lunch. Scali's memo goes up to the White House. After 6:00 p.m., Rusk tells Scali to answer that the U.S. sees possibilities. A long Khrushchev letter reaches the White House the same night | Khrushchev's letter reaches the U.S. embassy in Moscow at 9:43 a.m. Washington time, but takes more than 11 hours to reach the White House. Late that night Castro sends Khrushchev a telegram urging a nuclear first strike if the U.S. invades Cuba. Castro also orders Cuban forces to fire on any U.S. aircraft in Cuban airspace | [JFK Library](https://microsites.jfklibrary.org/cmc/oct26), [CFR, Day 11](https://www.cfr.org/articles/john-scali-has-lunch-with-a-soviet-spy-cuban-missile-crisis-day-eleven), [Scali memo (Avalon)](https://avalon.law.yale.edu/20th_century/msc_cuba085.asp) |
| 12 | Sat, Oct 27 | Black Saturday. See the next section | See the next section | [JFK Library](https://microsites.jfklibrary.org/cmc/oct27/) |
| 13 | Sun, Oct 28 | ExComm approves a statement welcoming Khrushchev's decision. Kennedy sends a reply and calls Hoover, Truman and Eisenhower | At about 9:00 a.m. Washington time, Radio Moscow broadcasts that the Soviet Union will dismantle and return the missiles. Castro is outraged | [JFK Library](https://microsites.jfklibrary.org/cmc/oct28/), [CFR, Day 13](https://www.cfr.org/articles/twe-remembers-jfk-and-khrushchev-agree-deal-cuban-missile-crisis-day-thirteen) |

## Black Saturday, October 27, 1962: one day, five places

The Defense Media Network article describes the day this way: by sunrise on the East Coast, [events that would almost cause a nuclear war were already happening](https://www.defensemedianetwork.com/stories/cuban-missile-crisis-50th-anniversary-black-saturday-agreement-and-lessons-learned/). A U-2 was heading over Cuba, another was heading for the North Pole, and an anti-submarine group was chasing Soviet submarines in the Caribbean.

### Part 1: The day in time order

This table puts the events on one clock. I only give a clock time where a source gives one. For the others I say "about" or describe the part of the day, and I flag what is missing.

| When | Where | What happened | Source and notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Overnight into the morning | Moscow to Washington | A second Khrushchev message arrives. Unlike the one the night before, it demands that the U.S. also remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey | [JFK Library](https://microsites.jfklibrary.org/cmc/oct27/). Defense Media Network says ExComm was shocked to find it when it met, and that [the second message had actually been sent first but delayed](https://www.defensemedianetwork.com/stories/cuban-missile-crisis-50th-anniversary-black-saturday-agreement-and-lessons-learned/). See the disagreement table below |
| 9:00 a.m. | Moscow Radio, heard in Washington | Radio Moscow begins broadcasting the Turkey demand | [CFR, Day 12](https://www.cfr.org/articles/black-saturday-threatens-a-calamity-as-president-john-f-kennedy-makes-two-offers-cuban-missile-crisis-day-twelve) |
| 10:00 a.m. | Washington, ExComm meeting 1 of 3 | CIA Director John McCone says five SS-4 missile sites are operational and a sixth will be ready within 24 hours. Kennedy learns a Soviet ship is 100 miles from the quarantine line, but Moscow has not been told where the line is. He decides to pass the location through UN Acting Secretary-General U Thant | [CFR, Day 12](https://www.cfr.org/articles/black-saturday-threatens-a-calamity-as-president-john-f-kennedy-makes-two-offers-cuban-missile-crisis-day-twelve) |
| During the morning meeting | Washington | A new Khrushchev letter arrives repeating the Turkey demand. Khrushchev argues that Turkey borders the Soviet Union just as Cuba is near the U.S. ExComm concludes that withdrawing the missiles under Soviet pressure would be a diplomatic disaster | [CFR, Day 12](https://www.cfr.org/articles/black-saturday-threatens-a-calamity-as-president-john-f-kennedy-makes-two-offers-cuban-missile-crisis-day-twelve) |
| Not confirmed: exact time | Over eastern Cuba | Major Anderson's U-2 is hit by a Soviet surface-to-air missile near the town of Banes. He is killed | [CFR, Day 12](https://www.cfr.org/articles/black-saturday-threatens-a-calamity-as-president-john-f-kennedy-makes-two-offers-cuban-missile-crisis-day-twelve) and [Defense Media Network](https://www.defensemedianetwork.com/stories/cuban-missile-crisis-50th-anniversary-black-saturday-agreement-and-lessons-learned/). Not confirmed: the sources I read give no clock time for the shootdown |
| Around midday | Washington | After his usual swim, Kennedy gets a call from Defense Secretary McNamara about a U-2 that has drifted into Soviet airspace | [CFR, Day 12](https://www.cfr.org/articles/black-saturday-threatens-a-calamity-as-president-john-f-kennedy-makes-two-offers-cuban-missile-crisis-day-twelve) |
| Around midday | Arctic, near Alaska and Siberia | Major Charles Maultsby's U-2 was collecting air samples near the North Pole. The northern lights disorient him, and he strays more than 300 miles into Soviet airspace. Soviet fighters scramble. The U.S. launches two F-102 fighters to escort him. They carry nuclear-tipped missiles because the U.S. is at DEFCON 2. Maultsby flies above what the Soviet fighters can reach and lands in Alaska on empty | [CFR, Day 12](https://www.cfr.org/articles/black-saturday-threatens-a-calamity-as-president-john-f-kennedy-makes-two-offers-cuban-missile-crisis-day-twelve) |
| Around midday | Washington | Kennedy's reaction to Maultsby, as CFR quotes it: "There is always some son of a bitch who doesn't get the word." By the time he said it, the plane had already left Soviet airspace | [CFR, Day 12](https://www.cfr.org/articles/black-saturday-threatens-a-calamity-as-president-john-f-kennedy-makes-two-offers-cuban-missile-crisis-day-twelve) |
| Afternoon into evening | Sargasso Sea, northeast of Cuba | A U.S. anti-submarine group chases Soviet submarine B-59, forcing it toward the surface with practice depth charges. B-59 is cut off from Moscow and its crew cannot tell if war has begun | [Defense Media Network](https://www.defensemedianetwork.com/stories/cuban-missile-crisis-50th-anniversary-black-saturday-agreement-and-lessons-learned/), [CFR, Day 12](https://www.cfr.org/articles/black-saturday-threatens-a-calamity-as-president-john-f-kennedy-makes-two-offers-cuban-missile-crisis-day-twelve) |
| 4:00 p.m. | Washington, ExComm meeting 2 of 3 | Kennedy learns Anderson is dead. General Maxwell Taylor recommends striking the missile site the next day. McNamara argues an invasion is now inevitable. Kennedy adjourns without deciding | [CFR, Day 12](https://www.cfr.org/articles/black-saturday-threatens-a-calamity-as-president-john-f-kennedy-makes-two-offers-cuban-missile-crisis-day-twelve) |
| Over the course of the day, with the decision to send Robert Kennedy made in the late afternoon | Washington | ExComm gravitates to the plan known as the "Trollope ploy": answer the friendlier October 26 letter and ignore the harsher October 27 one. In the late afternoon Kennedy decides to send Robert Kennedy to see Dobrynin | [CFR, Day 12](https://www.cfr.org/articles/black-saturday-threatens-a-calamity-as-president-john-f-kennedy-makes-two-offers-cuban-missile-crisis-day-twelve), [RFK memo](https://avalon.law.yale.edu/20th_century/msc_cuba096.asp) |
| Evening, local time | Sargasso Sea | B-59 surfaces. The USS Beale's deck log records the surfacing on the evening of October 27 | [National Security Archive](https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/briefing-book/russia-programs/2022-10-03/soviet-submarines-nuclear-torpedoes-cuban-missile-crisis). Arkhipov's own 1997 account says it was the night of October 27 |
| About 7:15 p.m. | Washington | Robert Kennedy phones Dobrynin and asks him to come to the Justice Department at 7:45 | [RFK memo](https://avalon.law.yale.edu/20th_century/msc_cuba096.asp) |
| 7:45 p.m. | Washington, Justice Department | The meeting begins. Robert Kennedy tells Dobrynin the U.S. must decide within 12 to 24 hours, that the missile bases must go, and that there can be no public deal over Turkey | [RFK memo](https://avalon.law.yale.edu/20th_century/msc_cuba096.asp) |
| 8:05 p.m. | Washington to Moscow | Kennedy's reply to Khrushchev's October 26 letter is sent as a telegram | [Telegram text](https://www.jfkthelastspeech.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Appendix-JFK-Telegram-to-Khrushchev-Oct-26.pdf), which says it comes from the JFK Library |
| Evening | Washington, ExComm meeting 3 of 3 | Kennedy approves activating 24 air reserve squadrons. He agrees that U.S. aircraft should return fire if reconnaissance planes are shot at again | [CFR, Day 12](https://www.cfr.org/articles/black-saturday-threatens-a-calamity-as-president-john-f-kennedy-makes-two-offers-cuban-missile-crisis-day-twelve), [JFK Library](https://microsites.jfklibrary.org/cmc/oct27/) |
| Night | Washington | Robert Kennedy records his brother's mood. The President "was not optimistic." The expectation was a military confrontation "by Tuesday and possibly tomorrow" | [CFR, Day 12](https://www.cfr.org/articles/black-saturday-threatens-a-calamity-as-president-john-f-kennedy-makes-two-offers-cuban-missile-crisis-day-twelve), quoting Robert Kennedy's memoir |
| Early hours of Sunday, Oct 28 | Moscow | Dobrynin's cable carrying Kennedy's offer reaches Khrushchev. He decides to answer over public radio to avoid delivery delays | [Defense Media Network](https://www.defensemedianetwork.com/stories/cuban-missile-crisis-50th-anniversary-black-saturday-agreement-and-lessons-learned/) |

### Part 2: The same day, place by place

| Place | What happened on October 27 | Why it nearly went wrong | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Washington | Three ExComm meetings (10:00 a.m., 4:00 p.m., evening). A new Soviet demand. A secret meeting with the Soviet ambassador. A decision to answer one letter and ignore the other | Kennedy's advisers were pushing for military action just as new Soviet demands arrived. Kennedy held off | [CFR, Day 12](https://www.cfr.org/articles/black-saturday-threatens-a-calamity-as-president-john-f-kennedy-makes-two-offers-cuban-missile-crisis-day-twelve) |
| Moscow | Khrushchev's second demand is broadcast. Later, he receives the Kennedy offer overnight | The U.S. side could not tell whether the Kremlin had hardened its position | [Defense Media Network](https://www.defensemedianetwork.com/stories/cuban-missile-crisis-50th-anniversary-black-saturday-agreement-and-lessons-learned/) |
| Cuba | Anderson's U-2 is shot down. Soviet short-range nuclear-armed cruise missiles are positioned about 15 miles from the U.S. base at Guantánamo Bay, under his flight path | Local Soviet officers feared he would see the deployment. CFR says they fired without waiting for Moscow | [CFR, Day 12](https://www.cfr.org/articles/black-saturday-threatens-a-calamity-as-president-john-f-kennedy-makes-two-offers-cuban-missile-crisis-day-twelve) |
| Arctic | Maultsby's U-2 wanders into Soviet airspace. Fighters from both sides scramble | The U.S. escort fighters carried nuclear-tipped missiles. The Soviets did not know why the plane was there | [CFR, Day 12](https://www.cfr.org/articles/black-saturday-threatens-a-calamity-as-president-john-f-kennedy-makes-two-offers-cuban-missile-crisis-day-twelve) |
| Sargasso Sea | B-59 is forced to the surface. Its captain wants to fire a nuclear torpedo | The U.S. Navy did not know the submarine carried one. Washington did not know about the incident until years later | [National Security Archive](https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/briefing-book/russia-programs/2022-10-03/soviet-submarines-nuclear-torpedoes-cuban-missile-crisis) |

### Part 3: The submarine, in plain English

The National Security Archive describes what happened on B-59. The submarine surfaced on the night of October 27 to charge its batteries. U.S. ships and planes were all around it. Arkhipov's own account lists planes flying 20 to 30 meters above the conning tower, searchlights, cannon fire, depth charges, destroyers cutting in front, and loudspeakers ordering the engines stopped.

According to an interview with another submarine captain, Ryurik Ketov, Savitsky believed war had started. He ordered an urgent dive and preparation of the nuclear torpedo. Arkhipov, who was still on the tower, saw that the Americans were signaling rather than attacking. He called the captain back and calmed him down. Savitsky's order was never passed to the officer in charge of the torpedo. The submarine signaled the Americans to stop, and the next day it dove and slipped away.

All of that comes from the [National Security Archive's 2022 collection](https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/briefing-book/russia-programs/2022-10-03/soviet-submarines-nuclear-torpedoes-cuban-missile-crisis). The Archive notes that Arkhipov, in his only known public statement, never used the word "nuclear" about the incident, and that the commanders suppressed the story for almost 40 years. Details became public through the 40th-anniversary conference in Havana in October 2002.

The U.S. Navy used "practice depth charges" to signal submarines to surface. The National Security Archive's document list includes a [U.S. Navy cable of October 24, 1962](https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/briefing-book/russia-programs/2022-10-03/soviet-submarines-nuclear-torpedoes-cuban-missile-crisis) setting out surfacing and identification procedures. A news article I read says that message never reached B-59, but I did not find a primary source for that claim. See the list of unconfirmed claims below.

## How the crisis ended (October 27 night to the following year)

| Date | What happened | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Night of Oct 27 | Kennedy's letter, delivered through Robert Kennedy, offers to end the quarantine and promise not to invade Cuba if the Soviets withdraw their missiles under verification. In the same meeting, Robert Kennedy privately tells Dobrynin the U.S. was planning to remove the Jupiter missiles from Turkey anyway. It could not be part of a public deal | [JFK Library](https://microsites.jfklibrary.org/cmc/oct27/), [State Dept.](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1961-1968/cuban-missile-crisis), [CFR, Day 12](https://www.cfr.org/articles/black-saturday-threatens-a-calamity-as-president-john-f-kennedy-makes-two-offers-cuban-missile-crisis-day-twelve) |
| Sun, Oct 28 | Khrushchev announces that the missiles will be dismantled and removed | [State Dept.](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1961-1968/cuban-missile-crisis) |
| Oct 28 | Kennedy's telegram expresses regret for the U-2 that strayed over Soviet territory. He also tells his brother, in CFR's account, that this is "the night I should go to the theater" (a reference to Lincoln) | [CFR, Day 13](https://www.cfr.org/articles/twe-remembers-jfk-and-khrushchev-agree-deal-cuban-missile-crisis-day-thirteen) |
| Oct 28 and after | Kennedy's public statement effectively ends the 13 days. Kennedy does not tell the three ex-presidents about the Jupiter promise | [JFK Library](https://microsites.jfklibrary.org/cmc/oct28/), [CFR, Day 13](https://www.cfr.org/articles/twe-remembers-jfk-and-khrushchev-agree-deal-cuban-missile-crisis-day-thirteen) |
| Following weeks | The quarantine continues until the Soviets agree to remove their IL-28 bombers. The U.S. ends the quarantine on November 20, 1962 | [State Dept.](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1961-1968/cuban-missile-crisis) |
| April 1963 | U.S. Jupiter missiles are removed from Turkey | [State Dept.](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1961-1968/cuban-missile-crisis) |
| Afterward | A direct White House to Kremlin telephone link, the "Hotline," is set up. Both sides take first steps toward a nuclear Test Ban Treaty | [State Dept.](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1961-1968/cuban-missile-crisis) |

## Where the sources disagree

History is messier than a clean timeline. Here is where the sources I read do not match.

| Question | One version | Another version | What I did |
|---|---|---|---|
| When was Kennedy first shown the proof? | State Dept.: the photos were presented to the White House on October 15 | A Foreign Relations of the U.S. summary: Bundy informed Kennedy at 8:45 a.m. on October 16. The JFK Library starts Day 1 on October 16 | I used October 16 for Kennedy personally and noted October 15 for the photos |
| Did Khrushchev's second message arrive overnight or on the radio? | CFR: Radio Moscow began broadcasting it at 9:00 a.m., and a letter arrived during the meeting | Defense Media Network: it had arrived overnight, and ExComm found it when they met. It also says the message was sent first but delayed | I reported both. The JFK Library says only that a second letter was received |
| When did the October 26 Khrushchev letter arrive? | State Dept.: sent in the evening, Washington time, which was the middle of the night in Moscow | CFR: delivered to the U.S. embassy in Moscow at 9:43 a.m. Washington time, then took 11 hours to reach the White House | I gave the CFR timing and flagged the difference |
| Who ordered the SAM shot at Anderson? | CFR: the local Soviet commander decided on his own, against Khrushchev's orders | A blog post I read (not a primary source) says two Soviet generals in Havana ordered it | I used CFR and flagged the dispute. Not confirmed from a primary source |
| Which U.S. ships were chasing B-59? | National Security Archive: the group built around the carrier USS Randolph, with the destroyers Beale and Cony | Defense Media Network says the torpedo was aimed at the USS Essex | I said "a U.S. anti-submarine group" and cited the Archive |
| What size was B-59's torpedo? | CFR: roughly the power of the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombs | Defense Media Network: a warhead of 15 to 20 kilotons | I did not give a number |
| Was Arkhipov's approval required to fire it? | CFR: the captain and political officer could normally have launched. Arkhipov's presence changed that | The National Security Archive notes that Arkhipov was the only eyewitness on the conning tower, and that the other submariners who confirm the story were not there for that exchange. A historian, Sergey Radchenko, argued in 2024 that Arkhipov's role rests on oral testimony (as reported on [Wikiwand](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Vasily_Arkhipov_(vice_admiral)), secondhand) | I described it as accounts from participants and flagged the debate |
| How much time was left before a U.S. strike? | RFK's memo to Rusk: decisions needed within 12 or possibly 24 hours | Defense Media Network: strikes and invasion in just over 36 hours | I quoted the memo, which is the primary source |
| How long until the Jupiters would go? | CFR: within six months | Defense Media Network: four to five months. RFK's own memo has a crossed-out sentence mentioning "four or five months" | I said "within months" and flagged the gap |
| Was the Turkey deal a trade? | RFK's memo says there could be no quid pro quo. The JFK Library chronology says there was an additional secret understanding | Dobrynin's cable describes an assurance that the missiles would be removed. The [National Security Archive](https://nsarchive.gwu.edu/nsa/cuba_mis_cri/moment.htm) notes that many people who studied the crisis later came to suspect Robert Kennedy had relayed a pledge | I reported the disagreement and did not pick a side |

## Claims I could not confirm

- **The exact time of the Anderson shootdown.** The sources I read give no clock time. One blog says Anderson took off at 9:09 a.m. from McCoy Air Force Base. I did not verify it, so I left it out.
- **That the F-102s were "within seconds" of launching nuclear missiles.** Only the Defense Media Network article says this. CFR says only that the fighters carried nuclear-tipped missiles and that, had they fought, those would have been their only weapons.
- **That the submarine never received the U.S. signaling message.** A news site claims it, but I found no primary document. The Navy cable of October 24, 1962 exists. I could not confirm whether B-59 received it.
- **Khrushchev's reasoning for settling.** Defense Media Network says he judged Kennedy's offer to be probably the best deal he would get. I could not confirm that from a Soviet primary source, so treat it as the author's inference.
- **Anything about the Soviet warheads in Cuba beyond the cruise missiles near Guantánamo.** One blog post says Soviet warheads were moved to the sites on October 26. I did not confirm it, so I left it out.
- **Casualty and cost claims from popular sites.** I did not use them.

## Why this still matters

The State Department's historians list two lasting results. First, both sides struggled to read each other during the crisis, which led to the Hotline. Second, both superpowers began to reconsider the arms race and took first steps toward a test ban treaty.

The Defense Media Network article adds two points of its own. It says the near-misses on October 27 shook leaders on both sides, which helped lead to better safeguards on nuclear weapons (it names Permissive Action Links). It also says the crisis showed how risky it is to keep forces on high alert near each other for weeks. These are that author's judgments, not settled fact.

My own take, and it is only mine: the most striking thing about October 27 is how many of the dangers were invisible to the people in the room. Kennedy was dealing with a letter, a shootdown and a stray plane. The Americans were not even aware at the time that B-59 carried a nuclear torpedo, and the story only became public decades later.
